name: Tata

profile.address: 1933, River Road, Osbornes Mills, Wall Township, Monmouth County, New Jersey, 07719
profile.reading: This site in the Osbornes Mills section of Wall Township, Monmouth County, sits at 1933 River Road near the Manasquan River, in a stretch of the Jersey Shore that has hosted transatlantic telecommunications cable infrastructure for decades. The property is identified with Tata, the Indian conglomerate whose telecommunications arm, Tata Communications, operates one of the world's largest wholly owned global network platforms, including a system of undersea fiber optic cables historically known as the Tata Global Network. Cable landing stations like this one are the onshore facilities where a submarine cable's fiber pairs come ashore, are terminated, and are connected into a carrier's terrestrial network. They are technical, low occupancy buildings built around cable terminating equipment, power feed equipment, and repeater monitoring gear, rather than the racks of customer servers found in a commercial colocation data center. Tata Communications does not publish a building specific data sheet, square footage figure, or power capacity for this station, which is standard practice for cable landing infrastructure across the industry. These are considered sensitive network assets, and operators generally limit public disclosure to the cable systems themselves rather than the physical stations that terminate them. No permit or capacity information for this specific address is publicly available. The facility remains a functioning piece of Tata's transatlantic network reach into the New York area, rather than a leasable data center in the conventional sense.

profile.duplicate_rationale: Same company as the canonical Tata Communications operator record (uid 5b5245af). This record is tied to the Wall Township, NJ cable landing station, which press sources identify as a Tata Communications facility.

reading:
This row duplicates the Tata Communications entry already held in this registry, and the single facility behind it is a subsea cable landing station rather than a data centre.

The building sits in Wall Township, Monmouth County, New Jersey, off River Road near Route 35, with a footprint of roughly 56,700 square feet on an industrial parcel of about five acres. Its map history explains how it arrived here. It was drawn in May 2020 as a plain building with no name. On 11 August 2026 a contributor named it Wall Township Cable Landing Station, set the operator to Tata and classified it as a telecom exchange. Eight days later the same contributor retagged a batch of cable landing stations from exchange to data centre. That reclassification, and not any Tata publication, is why a landing station now appears in a data centre registry with an operator row of its own.

The same edit left an alternate name reading Tata Cable Landing Station Tuckerton. Tuckerton is in Ocean County, about 40 miles south, and is a separate and well known New Jersey landing point. The alternate name conflates two distinct landing locations and should not be relied on for either.

The parcel is shared, and that is the more interesting fact. The neighbouring building, about 34,300 square feet, is mapped as the New Jersey Fiber Exchange at 1933 Route 35, operator NJFX, and a dedicated substation of about 5,700 square feet sits on the same parcel, with a mapped power cable route and a Jersey Central Power and Light distribution line running past. A reverse geocode of this row's stored coordinate returns the NJFX building rather than the landing station, because NJFX is the addressed and named neighbour. That is worth noting as a general caution: a reverse geocode answers with the nearest labelled thing, not with the thing being asked about. The stored coordinate itself does fall inside the landing station footprint.

NJFX publishes its own campus as a 64,000 square foot facility with 12 MW of power capacity, four subsea cables landing and more than 35 network operators present. Those figures describe the carrier neutral building next door, not this one. Tata publishes no square footage, no utility service size, no standby generator count and no IT load for the landing station itself, and none appears in any public filing found here. A cable landing station terminates subsea fibre and houses the power feed equipment for it. Presenting one as colocation capacity would misstate what the building does, and there is no basis for attributing megawatts of IT load to it.
